passages.title: What do fairy tales teach us?
passages.body:
What do fairy tales teach us?

Did you enjoy listening to fairy tales when you were younger? You may have
learnt a lot more than you think from these traditional tales...

Part 1

Children’s stories can help us understand the world, and fairy tales¹ provide ways [5]
for children to receive important messages. Although there are some themes in
fairy tales that are unrealistic, the overall effect is, I believe, important for
children’s development.

One way fairy tales help children develop is that they’re often written in a way
that encourages creativity. As well as reading the story, you can act it out, which [10]
helps to develop your imagination. Fairy tales and fables are also important for
teaching us the difference between right and wrong. And fairy tales and fables
teach us about being more in touch with nature and animals too. Have you ever
noticed how many of the fairy tales are set in the woods, in the countryside or
even in the sea? [15]

Fairy tales teach us life lessons wrapped in a story. In The Princess and the
Frog, we learn that we must try to give people a chance whatever their
appearance, while in Goldilocks and the Three Bears, we see that we should not
take things that don’t belong to us. The wolf in Little Red Riding Hood teaches us
about trust and that strangers can be dangerous. And, of course, in Pinocchio, [20]
we learn that we mustn’t tell lies.

These lessons teach us so many things about life, about friendship, and most of
all about love. Love is always the most powerful magic in every story. Children
learn from the characters in the stories, and this helps them connect the situation
with their own lives. The tales can show children how to have a positive outlook, [25]
especially if they have problems or feel anxious about something.

Part 2

Fairy tales teach children how to be creative. They also teach them about story
structure, story development and the description of characters – both heroes and
villains. Furthermore, fairy tales help children see the difference between fiction [30]
and non-fiction. They are, therefore, ideal for teachers to use in the classroom.

Like the magical characters they portray, fairy tales are not limited to a time or
place and can be found in many different cultures. India, for instance, has its own
Cinderella, as does China. Meanwhile, the 1000-year-old story of Little Red [35]
Riding Hood was famous in the Middle East centuries ago. But no matter where
the fairy tales came from, happy endings are an essential feature. We certainly
hope that Cinderella will find happiness. And in Snow White or Sleeping Beauty,
readers know that the princess will marry the prince and live happily ever after in
a palace. [40]

However, the world has changed a lot since the days of Cinderella. Some people
point out that feeding children a diet of fairy tales full of make-believe just isn’t
what they need. They argue that with a tough world out there, full of tricky
problems but not so full of enchanted frogs and fairy godmothers to resolve them,
children should read modern, realistic fiction that prepares them for everyday life.

Glossary

¹fairy tale: a children’s story with magical characters or set in magical places that
 has a happy ending

sections.title: Section A: Reading
sections.instructions: Spend 30 minutes on this section. Read the text in the insert, and answer Questions 1–9.

items.stem:
Look at the first paragraph in Part 1 (lines 5–8).

Give a two-word phrase from the first paragraph that tells us the writer is giving an opinion.
items.note: Mark scheme: I believe.

items.stem:
Look at the first paragraph in Part 1 (lines 5–8).

‘I’ is an example of a pronoun. Give one more pronoun from the first paragraph.
items.note: Mark scheme: us.

items.stem:
Look at the second paragraph in Part 1 (lines 9–15).

How does the writer connect the end of the first paragraph with the beginning of the second paragraph?

accepted: The writer mentions the importance of fairy tales for children’s development in both places
talks about children’s development in both
links children’s development in both paragraphs

items.note: Mark scheme: any answer conveying that the writer mentions / talks about / links the importance of fairy tales for children’s development in both places. A person should check this answer against the mark scheme.

items.stem:
Look at the second paragraph in Part 1 (lines 9–15).

Why is an apostrophe ( ’ ) used in the first sentence in this second paragraph?

accepted: to show a contracted verb form
to show the short form of they are
it is short for they are

items.note: Mark scheme: to replace a letter / a missing ‘a’; to show a contraction / contracted verb form; to show the short form of ‘they are’.

items.stem:
Look at the second paragraph in Part 1 (lines 9–15).

Look at the final sentence in this paragraph (lines 13–15). What kind of sentence is this?
items.note: Mark scheme: question.

items.stem:
Look at the third paragraph in Part 1 (lines 16–21).

Based on the information in this paragraph, match each fairy tale with its main message.
pairs: do not judge people based on how they look
be careful with people you don’t know
it is always better to tell the truth
items.note: Mark scheme: 1 mark each, maximum 4. On the printed paper a fifth message, ‘it is important to share what we have’, is offered and not used; this format has no unused option, so add it as a distractor in the editor if the sitting should keep one.

items.stem:
Look at the fourth paragraph in Part 1 (lines 22–26).

Look at lines 25–26. Write the conditional clause in this sentence.

accepted: if they have problems or feel anxious about something
especially if they have problems or feel anxious about something

items.note: Mark scheme: (especially) if they have problems (or feel anxious about something).

items.stem:
Now look at Part 2. Look at the first paragraph in Part 2 (lines 28–31).

Teachers use fairy tales to teach students about characters in stories and help develop their creativity. Give two other ways teachers use fairy tales.

accepted: story structure; the difference between fiction and non-fiction
to teach story structure and story development
story development and the difference between fiction and non-fiction

items.note: Mark scheme: 1 mark each, maximum 2 — to teach story structure; to teach story development; to show the difference between fiction and non-fiction. A person should check this answer against the mark scheme.

items.stem:
Look at the first paragraph in Part 2 (lines 28–31).

For is a preposition used in the first paragraph in Part 2. Give one more preposition.
items.note: Mark scheme: about / between / in.

items.stem:
Look at the first paragraph in Part 2 (lines 28–31).

Give one sentence opening that tells us the writer is adding more information.
items.note: Mark scheme: Furthermore, …

items.stem:
Look at the first paragraph in Part 2 (lines 28–31).

Give one sentence opening that tells us the writer is explaining something.
items.note: Mark scheme: They are, therefore …

items.stem:
Look at the second paragraph in Part 2 (lines 32–39).

Which verb does the writer use instead of ‘show’?
items.note: Mark scheme: portray.

items.stem:
Look at the second paragraph in Part 2 (lines 32–39).

Give one phrase that tells us that the Little Red Riding Hood fairy tale has been around for a long time.

accepted: famous in the Middle East centuries ago

items.note: Mark scheme: 1000-year-old story; (famous in the Middle East) centuries ago.

items.stem:
Look at the second paragraph in Part 2 (lines 32–39).

Was is an example of a past tense irregular verb. Give one other past tense irregular verb in this paragraph.
items.note: Mark scheme: came (from). Accept found.

items.stem:
Look at the third paragraph in Part 2 (lines 40–44).

Give one example of metaphor in this paragraph.

accepted: feeding children a diet of fairy tales

items.note: Mark scheme: … (feeding children) a diet of fairy tales.

items.stem:
Look at the third paragraph in Part 2 (lines 40–44).

Look at lines 42–44. What does tricky mean in this sentence?
items.note: Mark scheme: difficult.

items.stem:
Look at the third paragraph in Part 2 (lines 40–44).

Which word tells us that an animal is under a magic spell?
items.note: Mark scheme: enchanted (frogs).

items.stem:
Look at the third paragraph in Part 2 (lines 40–44).

Do you agree with the main idea in the final paragraph? Answer Yes or No, and give one reason for your choice.

accepted: Yes — it is more important to read realistic, modern stories
No — it is more important to read fairy tales

items.note: Mark scheme: 1 mark for an explanation that matches the answer given. Yes: reading realistic, modern stories is more useful. No: reading fairy tales and make-believe is more useful. A person should check this answer against the mark scheme.

items.stem:
Look at the whole text.

What do you think are the most important things that fairy tales can teach us about? Choose two of: dealing with our problems; using our imagination; telling the difference between right and wrong; describing characters.

Give reasons for your opinions using information from the text.

accepted: dealing with problems — fairy tales help me feel better about real situations; using our imagination — they help me make up other stories

items.note: Mark scheme: 1 mark for each reason that matches a choice made, maximum 2. Any valid reason. A person should check this answer against the mark scheme.

items.stem:
Look at the whole text.

How does the writer organise the information in the text?
items.note: Mark scheme: (The writer uses) paragraphs; (The writer uses) subheadings Part 1 and Part 2.

items.stem:
Your headteacher is suggesting that all students should spend 20 minutes a day reading fiction for pleasure and wants to know what you think of this idea.

Write a letter to your headteacher explaining what you think of this idea.

Think about:
• whether you agree with this idea
• when would be the best time of day to do this
• what sort of books you would like to read
• if there is anything else you would like to read
• whether reading for pleasure is important.

Remember to use the conventions of formal letter-writing.

Plan your letter first, then write it.
items.note: Marked with the Stage 3 writing grid: Creation of texts 5, Vocabulary and language 3, Grammar and punctuation 7, Structure of texts 7, Word structure (spelling) 3 = 25. 0 marks for 20 words or fewer; maximum 7 marks for 21–60 words.
